## Cylinder Sets

Cylinder sets are the basic building blocks of [[product-sigma-algebra|product
σ-algebras]] on infinite products such as $\mathbb{R}^T$, the space of all
functions $T\to\mathbb{R}$. A cylinder set restricts only *finitely many*
coordinates and leaves the rest free. They are how one builds a measure on a
space of paths from finite-dimensional information, as in
[[stochastic-processes]].

## Definition

Let $\{(X_t,\mathcal{M}_t)\}_{t\in T}$ be measurable spaces, $X=\prod_{t\in T}X_t$,
and for $S\subseteq T$ write $\pi_S:X\to X_S:=\prod_{t\in S}X_t$ for the
restriction $\pi_S(x)=(x_t)_{t\in S}$.

:::{.definition data-title="Cylinder Set"}

For a **finite** set $S=\{t_1,\dots,t_n\}\subseteq T$ and
$B\in\bigotimes_{t\in S}\mathcal{M}_t$, the **cylinder set** with base $B$ over $S$ is
$$
C_S(B):=\pi_S^{-1}(B)=\{x\in X:(x_{t_1},\dots,x_{t_n})\in B\}.
$$
If $B=E_{t_1}\times\cdots\times E_{t_n}$ with $E_{t_i}\in\mathcal{M}_{t_i}$ it is a
**measurable rectangle cylinder**, and if $n=1$ it is a **thin cylinder**
$\pi_t^{-1}(E)=\{x:x_t\in E\}$.

:::

:::{.example data-title="Coin Tosses"}

For infinitely many fair coin tosses, $X=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$, the event "the
first toss is heads and the third is tails" is the cylinder
$\{x:x_1=1,\ x_3=0\}$. The event "heads occurs infinitely often" is **not** a
cylinder, but is built from them using countable unions and intersections
(see [[limsup-liminf]]).

:::

A cylinder over $S$ with base $B$ is also a cylinder over any finite $S'\supseteq S$,
with base $B\times X_{S'\setminus S}$. This is the "padding" used to compare two
cylinders on different coordinates.

## Cylinders Form an Algebra

:::{.theorem data-title="Algebra of Cylinder Sets"}

The collection $\mathcal{C}$ of cylinder sets is an algebra of subsets of $X$.

:::

:::{.proof}
$X=\pi_S^{-1}(X_S)$ is a cylinder, and $\emptyset$ likewise. For the complement,
$C_S(B)^c=\pi_S^{-1}(B)^c=\pi_S^{-1}(B^c)=C_S(B^c)$ by
[[set-functions#Preimages Preserve Set Operations|preimages commuting with complements]].
For $C_S(B)$ and $C_{S'}(B')$ pad both to $S''=S\cup S'$ with bases $\tilde B,\tilde B'$.
Then $C_S(B)\cup C_{S'}(B')=\pi_{S''}^{-1}(\tilde B\cup\tilde B')\in\mathcal{C}$,
again as preimages commute with unions.
:::

In general $\mathcal{C}$ is **not** a σ-algebra when $T$ is infinite, since countable
unions can involve infinitely many coordinates.

## Generating the Product σ-Algebra

:::{.theorem data-title="Cylinders Generate the Product σ-Algebra"}

$\sigma(\mathcal{C})=\bigotimes_{t\in T}\mathcal{M}_t$. In fact the thin cylinders,
or the measurable rectangle cylinders, already generate it.

:::

:::{.proof}
The product σ-algebra is by definition generated by the thin cylinders
$\pi_t^{-1}(E)$, $E\in\mathcal{M}_t$, which are cylinders, so
$\bigotimes\mathcal{M}_t\subseteq\sigma(\mathcal{C})$. Conversely
$\pi_S:X\to X_S$ is measurable for the product σ-algebras: the generators of
$\bigotimes_{t\in S}\mathcal{M}_t$ are the coordinate sets $E$ in a single
coordinate $t\in S$, whose preimage under $\pi_S$ is the thin cylinder
$\pi_t^{-1}(E)$. By checking measurability on generators
([[set-functions#Preimages and σ-Algebras|here]]) every $\pi_S^{-1}(B)$ lies in
$\bigotimes\mathcal{M}_t$, so $\mathcal{C}\subseteq\bigotimes\mathcal{M}_t$.
:::

For uncountable $T$ the product σ-algebra is much smaller than one might expect.

:::{.theorem data-title="Countably Many Coordinates"}

Every set in $\bigotimes_{t\in T}\mathcal{M}_t$ is determined by countably many
coordinates: for each such $A$ there is a countable $S\subseteq T$ and
$B\in\bigotimes_{t\in S}\mathcal{M}_t$ with $A=\pi_S^{-1}(B)$.

:::

:::{.proof}
Let $\mathcal{A}$ be the collection of sets determined by countably many
coordinates. It contains every cylinder, is closed under complements (same $S$),
and under countable unions (take the union of the countably many coordinate
sets). So $\mathcal{A}$ is a σ-algebra containing the generators, hence contains
$\bigotimes\mathcal{M}_t$.
:::

:::{.example data-title="Non-measurable events in path space"}

On $\mathbb{R}^{[0,1]}$ with the product σ-algebra, the sets $C([0,1])$ of
continuous paths, $\{x:\sup_tx_t<1\}$ and the singleton $\{x_0\}$ for a fixed
path are not measurable, since none can be determined by countably many
coordinates. This is why constructing Brownian motion requires a continuity
argument beyond the extension theorem (see [[kolmogorovs-continuity-theorem]]).

:::

## Measures on Cylinders

Cylinder sets are the natural domain for specifying a measure from
**finite-dimensional distributions**.

- **Uniqueness.** Measurable rectangle cylinders are closed under finite
  intersections, so they form a $\pi$-system generating $\bigotimes\mathcal{M}_t$.
  By [[dynkins-pi-lambda-theorem|Dynkin's π-λ theorem]], two probability measures
  agreeing on all finite-dimensional rectangles agree on the whole product
  σ-algebra.
- **Existence.** Given a consistent family of finite-dimensional distributions
  $\mu_S$ (consistent meaning that marginalising $\mu_{S'}$ to $S\subseteq S'$ gives
  $\mu_S$), define $\mu_0(C_S(B))=\mu_S(B)$ on the algebra $\mathcal{C}$. For
  $X_t$ complete separable metric spaces (e.g. $\mathbb{R}$), the
  **Kolmogorov extension theorem** says $\mu_0$ is a premeasure, and the
  [[caratheodory-extension-theorem|Carathéodory extension theorem]] extends it to a
  unique measure on $\bigotimes\mathcal{M}_t$.
